MBIs are typically presented to clients as secular, scientifically validated treatments, yet their core techniques derive from Buddhist and other Eastern contemplative traditions (Creswell, 2017; Lee, 2018). A given intervention could therefore be framed to emphasize either its scientific or religious background. Davoodi and Lombrozo (2022) found that people assign different types of value to scientific versus religious explanations, attributing more epistemic merit (evidence, logic) to scientific explanations and more non-epistemic merit (social, moral relevance) to religious ones. Interestingly, religious participants in these studies gave more epistemic weight to religious explanations that aligned with their personal beliefs. If scientific and religious framings carry distinct evaluative weight for explanations and this weighting itself depends on the individual's religiosity, framings of MBIs may similarly interact with religiosity to shape how people evaluate them. The present research directly tests this possibility, examining whether scientific and religious framings of MBCT shape treatment acceptability, and whether this effect depends on participant religiosity.

In addition to religiosity (i.e., an individual's degree of commitment to and engagement with religious beliefs and practices), existential quest and scriptural literalism have been examined as predictors of MBI acceptability and treatment response. Existential quest reflects a construct that is rooted in Batson's (1976) "religion as quest" dimension of religion. According to Batson, high quest individuals are those who approach religion as an endless process of existential questioning without requiring clear-cut answers. Whereas Batson's existential quest dimension was centered specifically around religious belief, more recent measures have been designed to be administered to religious and non-religious individuals (Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012). In contrast, scriptural literalism means believing in the literal truth of a religion's sacred texts. Findings regarding these two constructs have been mixed across studies. Two studies reported by Palitsky et al. (2022) varied how an MBI was described to participants in the absence of an actual intervention. The MBI was described as secular, spiritual, Buddhist, or aligned with one's own tradition (most religious participants identified as Christian). Results showed that this framing moderated the association between existential quest and MBI acceptability, with a positive association within the Buddhist condition that replicated across two samples. Scriptural literalism predicted greater willingness to try mindfulness framed as spiritual or from one's own tradition, compared to when framed as secular or Buddhist. While these studies could not establish causality (all participants viewed all framings), the results suggest that existential quest and scriptural literalism relate to willingness to try an MBI in opposing ways, with existential quest favouring Buddhist framings and scriptural literalism favouring one's own religion.

However, in studies delivering a mindfulness intervention, existential quest and scriptural literalism showed inconsistent main and interaction effects on affective and acceptability outcomes across samples (Anderson et al., 2023; Palitsky et al., 2022): effects that emerged in one study often did not replicate in another. Building on this work, the present research tests whether existential quest and scriptural literalism interact with religious versus scientific framing to affect acceptability. Understanding such interactions can help healthcare providers use empirically informed strategies to increase client engagement.

In addition to how a potential client perceives the religious origins of MBIs, other aspects of treatment may pose barriers to treatment acceptability for participants, regardless of religion.

Unlike traditional one-on-one talk therapy, MBIs include solo meditation as well as group sessions, which may feel unfamiliar to or uncomfortable for participants (Lomas et al., 2015; Wahbeh et al., 2014). Indeed, people can be skeptical of MBI's credibility and deterred by their time demands, both of which reduce engagement (Marks et al., 2023). In addition to adjusting how an intervention is framed, directly addressing these structural and practical concerns when an intervention is first introduced may similarly improve acceptability. For example, providing clients with clear information about a treatment's expected length and likely course of clinical progress at the outset has been shown to improve treatment retention and completion (Swift & Callahan, 2011) Similarly, addressing the concerns of people referred to a crisis service increases their likelihood of using such referrals (Jaroszewski et al., 2019). Addressing barriers through tailored communication strategies may help increase the accessibility and appeal of MBIs, particularly for those who are skeptical or unfamiliar with these interventions. Thus, our second study tests whether addressing participants' specific concerns about MBCT, rather than adjusting how the treatment is framed, improves treatment acceptability.

The Current Studies

Study 1 (pre-registered: https://osf.io/zsmx4/overview) tested whether framing an MBI as scientific (emphasizing its basis in psychological research) or religious (emphasizing its South and East Asian origins) affects treatment acceptability. We also tested whether this association was moderated by religiosity. Participants were assigned to one of four conditions: Scientific framing, Religious framing, combined Religious and Scientific framing, or a Control framing for MBCT. After reading these framings, participants completed a treatment acceptability scale, provided open-ended reflections on why they would or would not be interested in MBCT, and questionnaire measures of existential quest, scriptural literalism, religiosity, and demographics.

Based on US demographics (Pew Research Center, 2025), we expected most participants to identify as Christian. Thus, we hypothesized that a Religious framing for MBIs would reduce treatment acceptability, whereas a Scientific framing would increase acceptability. We held no directional hypothesis for the interaction effect between Religious and Scientific framings on treatment acceptance scores. When adding religiosity as a moderator, we predicted an interaction between religiosity and framing, such that more religious individuals would rate acceptability lower, particularly when MBCT was framed religiously. Given mixed findings in prior literature (Anderson et al., 2023; Palitsky et al., 2022), we did not have a priori hypotheses regarding existential quest or scriptural literalism , and treated these as exploratory individual-difference measures.

We analyzed participants' open reflections on MBCT in Study 1 and discovered a set of nine common concerns that limited enthusiasm for MBCT (e.g., group format, time burden).

Study 2 (pre-registered: https://osf.io/xawkn) tested whether addressing these concerns would improve treatment acceptability. Participants read a description of MBCT and selected which of nine possible concerns they held about the proposed treatment. They were then assigned to one of three conditions that manipulated the response they received: Tailored Response (they saw responses that addressed only their selected concerns), Comprehensive Response (they saw responses that addressed all nine possible concerns), or No Response (no responses were given).

We hypothesized that participants in both the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions would report greater treatment acceptability compared to those in the No Response condition. Exploratory analyses for this study tested whether religiosity moderated acceptability outcomes and whether religiosity correlated with the strength of participants' initial concerns.

Study 1 Methods

Participants

We pre-registered (https://osf.io/zsmx4) a target sample size of 300 participants (75 per condition) based on a power analysis indicating that this sample would provide 80% power to detect small-to-moderate (f = 0.17) interaction effects in a 2 × 2 ANOVA. This sample size is also consistent with prior work examining how religious framing influences willingness to engage in mindfulness-based interventions (Palitsky et al., 2022). Participants aged 18-35 years were recruited through Prolific in July and August 2023. All participants were based in the USA.

We included a CAPTCHA and multiple-choice attention check question to screen for bots and inattentive participants. 328 participants completed the study and were approved for compensation; after excluding those who failed the attention check, our final usable sample consisted of 305 participants. This study was conducted in 2023, prior to the widespread use of AI tools, reducing concern that results reflect AI rather than human responses. Participant demographic data for Studies 1 and 2 can be found in Table 1.

Procedure

All study procedures were administered through Qualtrics. After providing informed consent, participants were given the following instruction: "Please imagine you are a patient dealing with an overwhelming amount of stress. After meeting with your primary health care provider you are recommended the following therapy to help improve your mental health." They were then randomly assigned into one of four between-subjects conditions: Religious (n = 80), Scientific (n = 80), Religious & Scientific (n = 75), or Control (n = 70). We detail these conditions below.

In all conditions, participants were presented with the same introductory description of MBCT. Depending on their condition, participants also read an additional explanation that manipulated how the origins of MBCT were framed (Table 2). These descriptions varied in a 2 [religious framing: present vs. absent] x 2 [scientific framing: present vs. absent] betweensubjects factorial design. This factorial design allowed us to examine the effect of each individual framing and whether the two might interact; for instance, whether the presence of a scientific framing could offset concerns raised by a religious one. The Religious condition emphasized the influence of Eastern religious traditions on MBCT, informed by prior work examining the historical and religious roots of mindfulness (Trammel, 2017). The Scientific condition highlighted its empirical and psychological foundations (Creswell, 2017). The combined Religious & Scientific condition contained both framings, with their order counterbalanced across participants to ensure that order would not influence outcomes.

Participants assigned to the Control condition did not read any additional text beyond the introductory MBCT description.

Table 2.

Study 1 MBCT Framing Manipulations.

Condition Framing

MBCT Introduction

Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) is an eight-week therapeutic program that can help people experiencing problems such as stress, anxiety, and depression. The therapy unites mindfulness training with cognitive therapy. Mindfulness skills are trained through weekly group sessions and guided meditations. These skills help people learn to pay attention to the present moment in a non-judgmental way. Cognitive therapy encourages individuals to become more aware of and less attached to their negative thoughts. MBCT connects these two techniques, helping people first notice and then let go of unhelpful thoughts in an accepting and non-judgmental manner.

Scientific Mindfulness in psychology is rooted in meditation and breathing techniques developed by 20th-century American Psychologists. Incorporating mindfulness into psychological therapies was first popularized in the 1970s with the creation of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Therapy. These psychological interventions often use meditation to improve a patient's attention and ability to focus on the present moment. Patients are also simultaneously taught to be less judgmental towards their fluctuating thoughts. From the scientific perspective, mindfulness interventions aim to help people be less critical of themselves and their thoughts allowing them to live a more peaceful non-judgmental life focused on the present moment. Mindfulness-based interventions are thus a tool for patients to improve their present-moment awareness and attention. Following these explanations, participants completed the Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale (Milosevic et al., 2015) as our primary measure of treatment acceptability. After this, they provided open-ended written feedback, explaining what influenced their interest or disinterest in MBCT. Then, participants completed questionnaires assessing religiosity (Centrality of Religiosity; Huber & Huber, 2012), existential quest (Existential Quest scale; Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012), and scriptural literalism (Truth of Text and Teaching; Streib et al., 2010), which were presented in a random order. Finally, participants completed a demographics questionnaire.

Measures

Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale (TAAS).

The Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Questionnaire (Milosevic et al., 2015) was used to measure participants' attitudes towards MBCT. This 10-item questionnaire uses a 7-point Likert scale to measure acceptability and adherence to a treatment, the primary dependent variable for this study. Higher scores indicate a stronger anticipated acceptability and commitment to the intervention. The TAAS demonstrates strong psychometric properties (Milosevic et al., 2015) and showed strong internal consistency in our sample, α = 0.93. The scale was originally designed for cognitive-behavioral interventions targeting fear and anxiety. Since no intervention was administered in the study, items related to fear and anxiety were adapted to focus instead on general mental health difficulties (see Supplementary Material Table S1).

Centrality of Religiosity Scale (CRS).

The CRS (Huber & Huber, 2012) was used as our primary pre-registered measure of religiosity. This 15-item scale assesses 5 characteristics of religious life: public practice, private practice, religious experience, ideological belief, and intellectual engagement. The CRS uses inclusive language to take into account a variety of religious traditions and beliefs. Responses are measured using a 5-point Likert scale, and the average of the scores serve as the religiosity score for each individual. Greater average scores indicate higher religiosity. The scale has been shown to have good reliability and validity (Huber & Huber, 2012) and showed strong internal consistency in our sample, α = 0.97. Note that item 7 of the questionnaire was unintentionally omitted from the study.

Existential Quest (EQ).

The Existential Quest scale is a nine-item survey used to measure an individual's flexibility in their existential beliefs (Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012). The scale uses a seven-point Likert Scale that highlights how open individuals are to religious and spiritual beliefs that are not their own. Higher existential quest scores reflect more openness to explore explanations for existential questions, and lower scores indicate greater attachment to one's current beliefs. The EQ scale shows good validity and reliability (Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012) and showed acceptable internal consistency in our sample, α = 0.74.

Truth of Text and Teaching (TTT).

The Truth of Text and Teachings scale is a fiveitem subscale of the Religious Schema Scale (Streib et al., 2010). we use this scale as a measure of scriptural literalism. TTT uses a seven-point Likert scale to measure how attached an individual is to the written stories and teachings of their religion. Those with higher scriptural literalism scores tend to view religious texts and teachings as absolute truth and interpret them more literally. This subscale shows strong validity and reliability (Streib et al., 2010) and showed strong internal consistency in our sample, α = 0.95.

Analysis Plan

To examine the effects of framing on treatment acceptability, we conducted a 2 [religious framing: present vs. absent] × 2 [scientific framing: present vs. absent] between-subjects ANOVA. As pre-registered, we conducted a second analysis that added religiosity as a moderator to the 2 × 2 ANOVA to test whether religiosity scores moderated the effects of framing on treatment acceptability.

We also conducted pre-registered exploratory analyses to test whether scriptural literalism and existential quest scores moderated the association between framing and TAAS scores. Two separate 2 × 2 between-subjects ANOVAs were conducted, each including TTT or EQ scores as a moderator, entered as both a main effect and in interaction with Scientific and Religious framing. A marginal interaction between existential quest and Scientific framing prompted post hoc, non-pre-registered exploratory analyses. Specifically, we conducted Spearman's correlations (because variables were not normally distributed) examining the association between existential quest and acceptability within each level of Scientific framing.

To explicate the relations between our two significant trait variables, we also conducted non-preregistered analyses testing whether existential quest and religiosity were correlated with one another, and whether each remained independently associated with acceptability when entered simultaneously in a combined model. Finally, we conducted non-pre-registered analyses of our key research questions within the N = 121 participants who identified as Christian to examine if these effects emerged within this subsample.

Qualitative responses to the open-ended question assessing participants' interest or disinterest in MBCT were analyzed using thematic analysis. The co-first authors independently reviewed participants' responses to identify recurring themes. After comparing initial coding schemes, co-authors agreed upon nine shared themes reflecting participants' concerns (see Table 3). Both then independently re-coded all responses for the presence of each of these nine themes, with disagreements resolved through discussion. Responses could include more than one theme.

Results

The pre-registered 2 × 2 between-subjects ANOVA revealed no main effect of Scientific framing, F(1, 301) = 0.56, p = .453, nor Religious framing, F(1, 301) = 1.16, p = .282, on treatment acceptability (Fig 1). The interaction between Scientific and Religious framing was also not significant, F(1, 301) = 0.002, p = .965. These results held when analyzing the subsample of N = 121 participants who identified as Christian, Fs < 2.53, ps > .114. TAAS = Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale. Error bars represent ±1 standard error of the mean.

When religiosity was added to the model as both a main effect and interaction term, there was a marginal main effect of religiosity, F(1, 297) = 3.65, p = .057, such that greater religiosity was associated with higher treatment acceptability across conditions. Neither the interaction between religiosity and Scientific framing, F(1, 297) = 1.23, p = .268, nor the interaction between religiosity and Religious framing, F(1, 297) = 0.30, p = .584, was significant. No main effects of Scientific framing, F(1, 297) = 0.41, p = .524, or Religious framing, F(1, 297) = 1.55, p = .214, were found. The three-way interaction between religiosity, Religious framing, and Scientific framing was also not significant, F(1, 297) = 2.64, p = .105. When analyzing only the N = 121 participants who identified as Christian, there was a significant main effect of religiosity, whereby greater religiosity was associated with greater acceptability, F(1, 113) = 6.24, p = .014. No other main or interaction effects were significant, Fs < 3.32, ps > .071.

Pre-registered exploratory analyses tested whether existential quest or scriptural literalism scores moderated the association between framing and treatment acceptability. In the model testing existential quest as a moderator, existential quest was significantly associated with treatment acceptability, F(1, 297) = 8.66, p = .004, such that higher scores were associated with greater acceptability. The Scientific × existential quest interaction effect was marginally significant, F(1, 297) = 3.13, p = .078. We unpacked this marginally significant interaction by examining the correlation between existential quest and treatment acceptability within each level of Scientific framing. A significant positive correlation emerged when Scientific framing was present, ρ(153) = .20, p = .01, but not when it was absent, ρ(148) = -.01, p = .873. No other effects were significant, ps > .162. In the model testing scriptural literalism as a moderator, no effects were significant, ps > .260.

In non preregistered correlation analyses, we found that existential quest and religiosity scores were correlated, ρ(303) = .13, p = .026. To examine whether the effect of religiosity was independent of existential quest, we entered both as simultaneous predictors, alongside framing, in a model predicting treatment acceptability. Both religiosity, F(1, 299) = 3.51, p = .062, and existential quest, F(1, 299) = 8.57, p = .004, retained similar effects as when they were modeled separately, indicating that each was independently associated with acceptability (though religiosity non-significantly). As above, the main effects of Scientific and Religious framing, and their interaction, were not significant, ps > .169.

Qualitative responses to the open-ended Reasons for Acceptability Ratings question were analyzed using thematic coding, yielding nine recurring themes reflecting participants' concerns (see Table 3). Fig 2 displays the frequency with which each theme was endorsed. Concerns about intervention efficacy and concerns that MBCT would require too much mental energy were the most frequently reported.

Fig 2. Percentage of Study 1 participants endorsing each concern.

Percentages are based on coding of participants' open-ended responses. Responses could be coded with more than one theme.

Discussion

Study 1 tested whether framing MBCT as having scientific or religious origins would affect acceptability of the treatment. Contrary to hypotheses, we found no main or interaction effects of scientific or religious framings, indicating that drawing attention to either the religious or scientific origins of MBCT does not seem to determine its acceptability by a prospective patient.

Religiosity showed a marginal independent association with acceptability, such that more religious participants rated MBCT as more acceptable. In participants who identified as Christian, this association was significant. These relationships held regardless of experimental condition (i.e., they did not interact with framing). Thus, religiosity appeared to shape baseline openness to MBCT independent of how it was introduced to participants, although the marginal significance of the overall effect means that it should be interpreted cautiously.

Existential quest, which reflects an individual's tendency to engage in existential questions about one's meaning, purpose, opinions, and goals in life, showed a significant positive association with acceptability. There was a marginal interaction between existential quest and Scientific framing in predicting acceptability, such that the association between existential quest and acceptability was significant when the Scientific framing was present but not when absent. Thus, participants with higher existential quest tended to find MBCT more acceptable specifically when it was introduced with a scientific framing; when participants received no scientific framing, existential quest was not associated with acceptability. Existential quest and religiosity were positively correlated, but even when adding them into the same model, existential quest remained significantly associated with acceptability, and religiosity remained marginally associated. Scriptural literalism showed no association with acceptability and did not interact with framing. We elaborate on how these results relate to prior work in the General Discussion.

Study 2

Taken together, findings from Study 1 suggest that acceptability of MBCT is shaped less by how the treatment is framed than by individual differences among participants. We reasoned that directly addressing concerns about the therapy, rather than shifting how it was framed, might offer a more promising route to increasing acceptability. Thus, Study 2 tested whether addressing the concerns participants raised in Study 1 would increase acceptability. We again measured religiosity in this study to provide yet another test of its relationship with MBCT acceptability and examine whether it interacted with our boundary-reduction intervention.

Methods

Participants

We pre-registered a target sample size of 705 participants (https://osf.io/xawkn). We aimed to match the sample size of Study 1, and given the availability of additional resources, we further increased the sample to maximize power to detect small effects in a one-way ANOVA (f = 0.12). Participants aged 18-35 were recruited using Prolific in March 2024. All participants were based in the US. Participants must have passed an initial CAPTCHA to access the study, and two attention checks were included during the study. First, after viewing the introduction to MBCT, participants completed a multiple-choice question asking which psychological therapy had been described. Second, participants reported how many portions of meat they typically ate per week and, later in the survey, were asked to indicate which food category they had previously been asked about. 767 participants completed the study; after excluding 62 participants who failed one or more attention checks, the final analyzed sample consisted of N = 705. As in Study 1, this study was conducted prior to the widespread adoption of AI tools, so results are unlikely to have been influenced by them. Participant demographic information is reported in Table 1.

Procedure

After providing informed consent and passing the CAPTCHA task, participants completed a survey administered via Qualtrics. As in Study 1, they were first instructed to imagine experiencing an overwhelming amount of stress and that their primary healthcare MBCT connects these two techniques, helping people first notice and then let go of unhelpful thoughts in an accepting and non-judgmental manner."

After reading this description, participants were shown the nine concerns that emerged from qualitative coding in Study 1 (Table 4). Participants were instructed to "Select all the concerns that you have with the proposed Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy" using checkboxes and could choose as many or as few concerns as they wished. For each item selected, participants then rated the extent of their concern on a continuous scale (0 = Not at all concerned,100 = Extremely concerned).

Next, participants were randomized into one of three conditions:

Tailored Response (n = 238), Comprehensive Response (n = 235), or No Response (n = 232). Minor deviations from our preregistered target of 235 participants per condition emerge due to excluding participants who failed attention checks after data collection was complete. Participants in the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions received a barrier reduction intervention inspired by Jaroszewski et al., (2019). In the Tailored Response condition, participants saw brief responses addressing only the concerns they had selected; if no concerns were selected, they proceeded directly to the next part of the study. Responses were written to be reassuring and informative while directly addressing each concern (Table 4). Participants in the Comprehensive Response condition received responses for all nine concerns, regardless of which they endorsed. Participants in the No Response condition received no additional information addressing their concerns. Subsequently, participants in the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions re-rated the extent to which they still held the concerns they originally selected, again on the 0-100 scale described above. Participants in the No Response condition did not complete this re-rating. Finally, all participants completed the TAAS, followed by an open-text question asking what interested or did not interest them about MBCT. Participants then completed the CRS and a demographics questionnaire. We did not include the EQ in this study because Study 2 was designed to test the effects of addressing participant concerns rather than to replicate the association between existential quest and acceptability in Study 1.

Measures

Treatment Acceptability and Adherence scale (TAAS). The adapted TAAS from

Study 1 was administered in Study 2 as our primary measure of acceptability of MBCT. The scale again showed strong internal consistency, α = 0.88.

Centrality of Religiosity Scale (CRS).

The Centrality of Religious Scale (CRS; Huber & Huber, 2012) was used to measure religiosity. All items of this scale were included in this study. The scale again showed strong internal consistency in this sample, α = 0.96.

Analyses

Our primary pre-registered analysis was a one-way ANOVA testing whether treatment acceptability differed across the three conditions. Pre-registered exploratory analyses further examined whether religiosity moderated treatment acceptability by including CRS scores as an interaction term in the ANOVA.

We also conducted a series of non-preregistered analyses to follow up on this initial test.

First, we were curious whether concern ratings changed from pre-to post-intervention in the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions, which we examined through paired t-tests for each of the nine concerns. Second, we observed that the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions both received a barrier-reduction intervention and their mean post-intervention acceptability scores were higher than the control condition. We thus combined them and conducted a non-pre-registered independent t-test comparing treatment acceptability in this combined Intervention group versus the No Response condition.

Finally, to explore the relationship between religiosity and specific concerns, we conducted pre-registered correlations between CRS scores and participants' initial ratings for each of the nine concerns.

Results

Our pre-registered one-way ANOVA revealed a marginal, non-significant effect of condition on treatment acceptability, F(2, 702) = 2.63, p = .073 (Fig 3; Control: M = 41.71, SD = 11.91; Tailored Response: M = 43.46, SD = 10.48; All: M = 43.90, SD = 10.29). When religiosity (CRS scores; mean-centered) was added to the model, there was a significant main effect of religiosity, F(1,699) = 11.08, p < .001, a marginally significant effect of condition, F(2,699) = 2.96, p = .052, and no interaction, F(2,699) = .326, p = .722. Given the similarity of post-intervention acceptability in the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions, we combined these groups into a single "Intervention" group. A non-pre-registered independent ttest showed that the Intervention group (M = 43.68, SD = 10.38) reported significantly higher acceptability than the No Response group (M = 41.71, SD = 11.91), t(407.54) = 2.15, p = .032, d = .18. Given the post-hoc nature of this comparison, this result should be interpreted only as preliminary evidence that responding to participants' concerns may increase treatment acceptability. TAAS = Treatment Acceptability and Adherence Scale. Error bars represent ±1 standard error.

The combined intervention conditions showed higher acceptability than the control condition.

Note, however, that the pre-registered one-way ANOVA across all three conditions showed only a trending effect (p = 073).

* p < .05

In both the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions, non-preregistered paired t-tests showed that concern ratings decreased from pre-to post-intervention for eight of the nine concerns, 4.27 < ts < 13.73, ps < .001, ds > .55 (Fig 4). Interestingly, ratings for the religious concern did not significantly change, t(14) = 2.08, p = .057, but this was also the least frequently endorsed concern (n = 15; counts presented in the Supplementary Material Table S2). Data are from the Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals. Each concern was rated only by participants who endorsed it, and n above each pair of bars shows the number of participants who endorsed it. Brackets show paired t-tests comparing pre-and post-intervention ratings. *p < .05; †p < .10.

Because religiosity scores were not normally distributed, we used Spearman correlations to examine associations between religiosity and initial concern ratings. This revealed a significant negative correlation for the group setting concern, ρ(439) = -.13, p = .007. No other correlations reached significance, ps > .101 (Supplementary Material Table S3).

Discussion

Study 2 sought to understand whether addressing participants' concerns with MBCT would increase treatment acceptability. Although a one-way ANOVA across all three conditions showed only a trending difference in treatment acceptability, a post-hoc analysis showed that acceptability was higher when the two intervention conditions were combined and compared to the control condition.

We found that concern ratings dropped significantly from pre-to post-intervention for all concerns except the religious concern, which did not significantly change and was the least endorsed concern (potentially reducing power to detect an effect). Thus, the barrier reduction responses provided in Table 4 were overall effective at addressing participants' concerns, but additional tests are needed to ensure that is the case for the response to religious concerns.

In Study 1, religiosity showed a marginal positive association with acceptability, and here we found that this relationship was significant, regardless of what condition participants were assigned to. This result suggests that religiosity reflects a general openness toward mindfulnessbased approaches rather than one activated by specific framing or intervention content. More religious individuals additionally demonstrated lower concerns about the group-based format of MBCT, potentially due to familiarity and comfort with group discussions of emotional and/or spiritual concerns.

Together, these findings suggest that directly addressing individual concerns is effective at reducing them, and modestly increases overall treatment acceptability relative to not receiving an intervention. More religious individuals were more receptive to MBCT regardless of intervention content, pointing to religiosity as a stable individual difference worth considering in how mindfulness-based interventions are introduced and tailored to prospective clients.

General Discussion

Identifying strategies to increase potential clients' interest in receiving MBIs is important for maximizing the positive impact of these interventions (Khoury et al., 2013). Study 1 examined whether framing MBCT as religious or scientific would affect its overall acceptability, and whether religiosity would moderate this relationship. Framing had no effect on acceptability, and religiosity did not moderate the effect of framing. However, religiosity showed a marginal positive association with acceptability overall, suggesting more religious individuals may be more receptive to MBCT regardless of how it is introduced. The presentation of MBCT (across conditions) as rooted in meditation, present-moment awareness, and non-judgmental acceptance, may resonate with contemplative practices common across religious traditions (Walsh & Shapiro, 2006).

There are two key sets of results to review from the studies presented here. The first set are from the results regarding framings and religiosity self-report variables. Based on prior work (Davoodi & Lombrozo, 2022; Palitsky & Kaplan, 2021), we hypothesized that emphasizing the religious origins and aims of MBCT might reduce US-participants' interest (due to conflicts with their primarily-Christian identification; Pew Research Center, 2025), whereas emphasizing the scientific origins and aims of MBCT might enhance interest. We included each as separate factors to test whether they may interact. Curiously, we found no significant differences across any of these conditions. Unlike (Palitsky et al., 2022): Framings did not influence acceptability scores. On the one hand, this suggests that there are no major impacts of how providers introduce mindfulness interventions. On the other hand, these null effects may have emerged due to limitations in our sampling and methods, a point we return to later.

Although differences in framing across conditions did not affect acceptability, we did find that two key religious variables were related to acceptability of MBCT. First, existential quest (i.e., a person's tendency towards flexible engagement with existential questions) showed a robust association with acceptability. Having high existential quest may provide a conceptual fit with MBCT, as the therapy encourages individuals to observe thoughts non-judgmentally and to engage in present-moment awareness, paralleling the open, curious stance that characterizes existential quest (Kabat-Zinn, 2003; Van Pachterbeke et al., 2012). Thus, high existential quest individuals may themselves be good candidates for this type of therapy, Further, enhancing the psychological perspectives underlying existential quest may help boost potential clients' willingness to engage with mindfulness interventions. Interestingly, the marginal interaction between existential quest and Scientific framing indicated that the association was stronger when MBCT was framed scientifically than when it was not. This pattern contrasts with Palitsky et al.

(2022), who found that existential flexibility was associated with greater MBI acceptability specifically under Buddhist framing. Our results instead align with findings from Anderson et al. (2023), who found that existential quest predicted more favorable responses to a brief mindfulness intervention specifically within a secular framing condition. It is possible that our religious framing's emphasis on "transcend[ing] one's human boundaries" and "connect[ing] to an otherworldly unifying force" weakened the existential quest-acceptability association among individuals who favor open engagement with existential questions. However, this interpretation should be taken cautiously, given the marginal results and exploratory nature of the analysis.

Nonetheless, religiosity was marginally associated with acceptability in Study 1 (and this association was significant in Christian participants) and significantly associated with acceptability in Study 2. Religiosity did not interact with condition in either study. This pattern was surprising, given concerns in the literature that MBCT's roots in Eastern religious traditions might make it less acceptable to religious individuals, particularly those from monotheistic backgrounds (Knabb, 2012; Palitsky & Kaplan, 2021). One explanation for the pattern we observed is that MBCT's core practices, present-moment awareness and non-judgmental acceptance of one's thoughts, overlap with contemplative traditions found within many religions, including Christian silent, contemplative prayer (Knabb, 2012). More religious participants may therefore view MBCT as compatible with, rather than in conflict with, their existing spiritual practice. Religiosity was also associated with lower concern about the group-based format of MBCT, which may reflect greater familiarity with communal practice among more religious participants. Our results align with prior research suggesting that Christian participants have a greater preference for group, couple, and family therapy environments compared to participants unaffiliated with a religion (Schultz et al., 2025).

Study 1 clarified that religiosity associations were not attributable to covariance with existential quest. Although they shared a small positive correlation, adding them into the same model did not alter the significance of their associations with acceptance. This suggests that, despite some overlap, existential quest and religiosity reflect distinct routes to finding MBCT acceptable, one rooted in existing religious beliefs, and the other in an exploratory stance towards meaning and existential questions. Interestingly, scriptural literalism showed no association with acceptability and did not interact with framing, aligning with one of Palitsky et al.'s (2022) experimental intervention studies, but diverging from their cross-sectional studies and findings from Anderson et al. (2023). Thus, findings regarding scriptural literalism are mixed across studies, suggesting that differences in framing content, wording, and sampling across studies may influence results.

The second set of results that merit discussion are the specific concerns participants raised and the techniques one can use to mitigate those concerns. In Study 1, allowing participants to describe their reactions to MBCT in their own words revealed a set of recurring nine concerns. The most common was doubt about treatment efficacy, while concerns regarding religion were the least frequent. Study 2, drawing on methods from Jaroszewski et al. (2019), then tested whether addressing all concerns or only a participant's selected concerns would increase acceptability relative to a no-intervention control. Notably, addressing participants' concerns substantially reduced the intensity of all but one item, indicating that the intervention was effective at reducing concerns. Thus, the short responses we provide in Table 4 could be deployed at a larger scale to help reduce barriers to MBCT engagement. Interestingly, concerns relating to religion were numerically (but not significantly) reduced following this intervention.

This null effect may reflect limited power given that it was the least endorsed item, consistent with religion also being the least frequent concern in Study 1, or that hesitations rooted in religious incompatibility are less responsive to brief reassurance than other practical concerns.

The finding that religion was the least frequently endorsed concern in both studies suggests that it is not a common barrier to engaging with MBCT, whereas concerns regarding time commitment and group-based format may be more important to address given how frequently they were raised.

Importantly, when the two concern-addressing conditions (Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response) were combined, participants in this intervention group reported significantly higher acceptability than those in the control condition. Thus, addressing concerns not only reduced how strongly participants endorsed those concerns, but also had a small effect on increasing treatment acceptability. The Tailored Response and Comprehensive Response conditions did not show different effects, suggesting that addressing only a participant's selfselected concerns is as effective as addressing all possible concerns. Our results suggest that, in practice, intervention providers could either respond specifically to the concerns that a prospective client raises, or provide standardized information covering common concerns, without sacrificing effectiveness. However, this effect should be interpreted cautiously given that the effect was small and emerged only when the two intervention conditions were combined.

In terms of strengths, both studies benefited from pre-registered experimental designs and well-powered samples, drawn from a representative pool of young U.S. adults. However, there remain several limitations to the study. First, our participants were not clinical samples who were seeking treatment. The responses of a non-clinical sample thus may not reflect how prospective clients seeking treatment would evaluate a real MBCT intervention. Second, we used a hypothetical intervention; participants did not have any real contact with a clinician or therapist.

It is possible that framings or concern responses provided during a live intervention would show greater effects on acceptability than what we found. Third, we measured acceptability rather than behaviors to pursue or engage with treatment. Thus, our results cannot speak to whether greater acceptability ratings are associated with greater likelihood of engaging with treatment. Fourth, our samples were predominantly Christian and agnostic/atheist, limiting generalizability to other religious groups. Relatedly, our measure of religiosity (CRS) may not capture orientations of participants who do not take part in organized religion, including those who identify as spiritual but not religious. Future research could address these limitations by recruiting clinical samples engaging in real interventions, measuring engagement with the intervention, recruiting more religiously diverse samples and including measures of spirituality. Doing so would help clarify how framing, concern-addressing, and individual differences such as religiosity and existential quest shape engagement with MBIs.

Together, these studies suggest that while framing MBCT as religious or scientific did not shift overall treatment acceptability, but directly addressing participants' concerns did improve acceptability relative to no intervention at all. Our findings suggest that perceived religious framing of MBIs may not provide a barrier to initial acceptance of a treatment, and they point to concern-focused intervention as a more promising avenue for increasing acceptability.

Interestingly, studies showed that religiosity and existential quest were associated with greater acceptability of MBCT, providing new data suggesting that certain aspects of mindfulness-based interventions may actually be appealing to these individuals. However, some effects differ from those found in prior studies, prompting further study in more naturalistic contexts. Nonetheless, these studies provide new guidance on ways for clinicians and researchers to best minimize client concerns and engage clients who may be most willing to utilize mindfulness-based interventions.

Religious

Mindfulness is rooted in meditation techniques developed by South and East Asian religions. Meditation practices have been passed down for centuries, being recorded as early as 1500 BCE. These traditions often see meditation as a way to transcend one's human boundaries and connect to an otherworldly unifying force. To reach this state one must develop heightened levels of attention and awareness to their surroundings. From this religious perspective, mindfulness interventions aim to help people see and understand the true impermanent nature of the world and reach a form of enlightenment. Mindfulness-based interventions are thus a tool for patients to progress toward greater spiritual insight and peace of mind. Note. Scientific condition = Introduction + Scientific framing; Religious condition = Introduction + Religious framing; Combined condition = Introduction + Scientific and Religious framings (order counterbalanced), Control condition = Introduction only.

Briefly explain what interested you or disinterested you about the therapy." Responses were analyzed using thematic analysis (see Analysis Plan).

The evidence suggests that MBCT can help individuals develop healthy coping mechanisms that are nonjudgemental and accepting. Learning to use these skills in response to challenging situations and everyday life can enhance your mental well-being.Instructors know that people are often worried about the difficulty of the treatment, so they start "at square one." Therapists will teach you ways to help learn the basics of mindfulness, and daily exercises are given to encourage you to practice and refine these skills. So even if there are challenges, MBCT creates a space for you to have the opportunity to improve your mental capabilities and in no way expects you to come with these skills refined.Some might prefer medication over therapies like MBCT. Medication can be an effective component of mental health treatment, and you do not have to avoid medication to practice MBCT. MBCT offers a non-pharmacological approach that can complement or offer an alternative to medication. Depending on your needs and preferences, MBCT can be used in conjunction with medication. In fact, for some people, a combination of MBCT with medication might be the most effective approach for improving mental health.The unique structure of the intervention provides you with guidance from a trained therapist and exercises you can practice in the comfort of your own home. The group sessions also allow you to support and feel supported by other people. Thus, MBCT may offer a more positive experience of mindfulness compared to what you may have tried before.Although group sessions might seem stressful, they are mediated by a professional therapist who guides sessions and helps you benefit from group interactions in ways be uncomfortable for me you might not receive through 1:1 intervention. For example, group sessions can provide you with emotional support and understanding. Group members learn from one another and build a sense of community that can make therapy rewarding and manageable. The presence of other participants can also offer motivation to engage in and complete therapy exercises.need to replace your existing coping strategies. It can be an additional tool for improving your mental wellbeing. The skills learned in MBCT can complement and enhance your existing strategies, offering new techniques for managing mental health. In general, having a larger "toolkit" for managing your mental health can provide you with more benefits as you will have a broader, more diverse set of skills to handle your mental well-being.that opening up about private matters might be uncomfortable and they will help you to share as much as you feel comfortable with. MBCT can help you become aware of and observe the thoughts that make this scary for you, allowing you to overcome them and grow more secure in these spaces. The group sessions are designed to be a confidential place where you can voice your experiences if and when you feel comfortable doing so.Mindfulness practices have some roots in religious and spiritual traditions, which might raise concerns for those wary of these elements. However, in the context of MBCT, mindfulness is taught through the lens of a non-religious psychological tool that has strong scientific support. The focus of this program is on the practical application of mindfulness for better managing your thoughts and emotions and improving mental well-being. Thus, MBCT is accessible regardless of your cultural, religious, or spiritual background.
